Topic at a glance
Environmental Impact Assessment — Screening, Scoping, Consultation, Clearance and Monitoring is a registered theme in Environmental Law. Environmental Impact Assessment — Screening, Scoping, Consultation, Clearance and Monitoring is governed by Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Water Act, 1974; Air Act, 1981; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010; and constitutional environmental principles. identify the environmental medium, applicable statute, consent or clearance, limitation and the competent forum; distinguish statutory relief from constitutional public-interest remedies.

cases.name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
cases.facts: The Court addressed a hazardous industry gas leak and public-law consequences.
cases.issue: What liability follows from hazardous industrial activity causing environmental harm?
cases.ratioDecidendi: An enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community and cannot rely on the traditional exceptions to strict liability.
cases.holding: The Court developed the Indian absolute-liability rule.
cases.relevance: Use for hazardous activity, compensation and environmental liability.

cases.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
cases.facts: Industrial pollution from tanneries affected water, soil and community health.
cases.issue: Whether sustainable development and precautionary environmental principles form part of Indian law.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle are part of Indian environmental law and must inform judicial and administrative action.
cases.holding: The Court directed remediation and compliance with environmental principles.
cases.relevance: Use for precaution, polluter pays and sustainable development.

cases.name: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath
cases.facts: A private project affected a river and public ecological resources.
cases.issue: Whether the State may permit private appropriation of public-trust resources.
cases.ratioDecidendi: The State holds natural resources in trust for the public and cannot abdicate that fiduciary obligation.
cases.holding: The public-trust doctrine was applied to environmental protection.
cases.relevance: Use for public trust, rivers, forests and ecological commons.
